Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.

- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. So a 4K-era forecast scored against the 16K final value, as in H1 and H4 of the forecast linked above, starts about 0.03 high from the packing change alone. The offset may also drift over the remaining 16K training, so if it's cheap, one 4K eval of the final checkpoint would let these forecasts be checked at the 4K packing they were built on. How I'll compare the forecasts at the end, fixed before phase 2, is in [this addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/phase2-plan-2026-10-22/addenda/2026-10-22_phase2_plan.md).

We will re-eval all checkpoints at 4k seqlen once the run is done, for those who have been tracking separate predictions. (Though a model trained at 4k->16k->65k may eval slightly differently at 4k than one that stayed at 4k the whole run, so not making any claims from our end on where that will end up).

A heads-up for the hero's planned 262K extension (#10618): with evals packed at the training context, Paloma's PTB and WikiText-103 val sets are each shorter than one 262,144-token sequence, so they yield no eval data ([`tokens // seq_len`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L93)). Their losses are then logged as 0.0 and the Paloma group macro skips them ([eval.py#L634-L636](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L634-L636)), so `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` silently becomes a 14-subset mean: at current values a jump of about +0.06 (about 3%), enough to trip `eval_regressed`. The top-level `macro_loss` instead averages the zeros in ([eval.py#L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L611)), about −0.14 on the hero's 23 tags. The 67B's 65K→262K switch, with the same tokenizer and Paloma files, shows both: from step 155,999 ([65K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k)) to 156,000 ([262K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k)), `eval/paloma/macro_loss` rose 2.1774 → 2.2150 while the other 14 subsets moved +0.0004, and `eval/macro_loss` fell 2.0260 → 1.8607 (2.0379 without the zeros). Either fix is small: mask zero-token tags in the top-level macro as the group macros already do, or keep all 16 subsets by setting `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` (#9890) to 65,536 for the 262K phase.

🤖 Confirmed in the current source: [`TokenSeqDataset.async_len`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L92-L93) drops partial sequences, and [`TaggedEvaluator.evaluate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L608-L636) includes empty tags in the overall macro while excluding them from group macros. I will exclude zero-token tags from the overall loss and bits-per-byte macros, and cap eval packing at 65,536 tokens in the Hero scaling-ladder and diagnostic launchers so the 262K phase retains all 16 Paloma subsets. This is a separate follow-up to #10618; it requires no live run change.

🤖 Implemented in #10711: zero-token tags are excluded from the overall loss and bits-per-byte macros, and Hero scaling-ladder/diagnostic eval packing is capped at 65,536 tokens to retain all 16 Paloma subsets during 262K training. Configuration checks cover 4K, 16K, 65K and 262K. The affected CPU suite passed 3,297 tests; its one Linux-only bubblewrap failure also reproduces on base commit 8577d25821 on macOS. Formatting, type checking and advisory review completed with no findings. This is a code change for review; the live Hero run has not been changed.
@ClassicLarry ^^ unclear if this is how we want to handle it. really we want separate long context ppl evals but we didn't set that up in time reliably.
i'll just add all lengths eval and that'll fix our paloma plots too

🤖 Updated #10711 to evaluate 4K, the current training length, 65K and 262K at every scheduled eval on the next Hero relaunch, with duplicate lengths removed and separate metric series. Continuous-text validation now pads and masks its final partial sequence, so short corpora remain in the 262K aggregate; the 65K cap has been removed. The unqualified Hero loss still reports the training-length eval. Dropless evaluation adjusts its batch/context layout to preserve tokens per eval batch.

The updated affected CPU suite passed 3,574 tests; the only failure remains the independently reproduced Linux-only bubblewrap test on macOS. Lint, type checking and advisory review passed. Multi-device tests cover long evals, masked short corpora and the return to training. No run was relaunched; GPU peak memory and wall time still need a rehearsal.

🤖 #10711 now defers eval contexts above the current training length. The next relaunch's current config evaluates 4K and 16K with separate metrics; fixed 65K and 262K series are added as training reaches those lengths. topics.head: eea42ac9a3a197345bf6f762709fb6aed7c0e0aa
topics.body:
Hero evals score 4K and the current training length, adding fixed 65K and 262K evals only once training reaches those lengths. Each distinct length has its own metrics, such as `eval_dropless/seq_len_4096/paloma/macro_loss`; `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` continues to report the training-length eval.

All eval lengths keep the training context-parallel width. The dropless mesh and PartitionSpec renaming reuse #10709's implementation: each device retains its training context group and uses its training (data, expert) group for eval data. Eval therefore reuses the device groups whose replacement caused NCCL memory growth in #10709. Batch sizes stay within the configured global padded-token budget per evaluation batch, rounded down to whole batch shards.

Continuous-text validation retains incomplete final sequences with right padding and excludes padding from attention and loss, including the real-to-pad prediction. Short Paloma corpora remain in the long-context aggregate. Validation sequence statistics include the final partial sequence; stored token counts exclude padding. Overall loss and bits-per-byte macros exclude tags with no scored tokens.

CPU tests check device groups, per-device parameter shards and the multi-length eval-to-training handoff. No GPU rehearsal of this revision has run.

Part of #8435.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f.

The change scores the hero at 4K, 65K, 262K and the training length at every scheduled eval. It also stops validation from dropping each continuous-text corpus's final partial sequence. The Levanter padding and macro-average changes are sound and well tested. The one design problem is in the hero: the dropless eval for the long lengths runs on a mesh whose device groups training never uses. Open PR #10709 measured that pattern exhausting GB200 memory.

**Before.** `_run_grug_local` built at most two evaluators at a single length: `cb_tagged_evaluate` on the training mesh and a dropless evaluator on `compact_grug_mesh(expert_axis_size=1, context_axis_size=<training CP>)`. `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` could pin that length, but no launcher set it. Validation used `TokenSeqDataset`, which drops the incomplete tail, so a Paloma subset shorter than one sequence (PTB, WikiText-103 at 262K) yielded no examples. The macro then averaged a zero-weight tag into the result.

**Design.** `build_eval_hooks` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:701`) builds one hook per length and backend. Every hook holds the training-length token budget, `eval_batch_size * train_seq_len`. `_dropless_eval_mesh` reshapes each rack's `(data, context, expert)` devices into a wider `context` axis when one sequence per batch shard would exceed that budget. At the 16K hero this yields CP1/CP1/CP4/CP16 for 4K/16K/65K/262K. Metrics go to `<prefix>/seq_len_<n>/…`, and the training-length hook also writes the old unqualified keys. In Levanter, `PaddedTokenSeqDataset` right-pads the tail and adds `valid_tokens`. `CausalLmDataset` turns those into segment ID `-1` and zero loss weight, including the real-to-pad prediction. FA4's packed-segment bounds already treat `-1` as invalid. `TaggedEvaluator` excludes tags with no scored tokens from both macros.

**Evidence and limits.** I ran the new tests locally on CPU and all 11 passed: `test_evaluation.py`, the padded-validation cases in `test_text.py`, and the macro test in `test_eval.py`. The PR body says GPU memory and wall time are unmeasured, and the README asks for a rehearsal before the relaunch. Nothing exercises the CP4/CP16 eval meshes on GPUs, or the `_fa4_cute.py` unit-batch normalization outside its CPU path.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:634` `_dropless_eval_mesh` gives the 65K and 262K evals device groups that 16K CP1 training never uses. The 65K eval has CP4 groups of four adjacent devices and data groups of 16. The 262K eval has CP16 and data 4. Open #10709 (mcwitt) measured this mechanism on the same model. XLA creates an NCCL communicator for each new group, keeps it outside the allocator pool for the rest of the process, and at 65K CP4×EP16 that added about 7.4 GiB per GPU against 5.8 GiB of headroom, so the next train step failed to allocate. Here the two long-length evals each add a new layout at every scheduled eval, so the first eval of the relaunched hero can OOM its next train step. #10709 also rewrites the same dropless-mesh code (`expert_collapsed_eval_mesh` plus a spec-renaming `_reshard_tree_to_mesh`), so the two PRs conflict. Land #10709 first, then rebase this PR onto its fold for each length whose context width equals training's. Keep 65K and 262K out of `HERO_FIXED_EVAL_SEQ_LENS` (`hero_recipe.py:35`) until a one-rack rehearsal records non-pool memory across those evals and the next train step. If a raised-CP length does not fit, score it from checkpoints in a separate eval job.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py:562` `remainder` defaults to `"drop"`, and `count_corpus_sizes` (`datasets.py:1414`) still builds validation sets without it. So `data/stats/validation/<name>/total_seqs` now counts one sequence fewer than the evaluator scores for every corpus with a partial tail, and zero for the short Paloma subsets this PR keeps. Make `remainder` a required keyword, as AGENTS.md asks for critical parameters, and pass `remainder="pad"` for the validation loop in `count_corpus_sizes`.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f -->

🤖 Removed stale expert-collapsed wording from the shared eval hook. The two review findings change behavior and remain open. Pre-commit, 11 focused CPU cases, and lint review passed. Commit 70df5e5f93.

<!-- marin-deslop:cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f -->

🤖 Addressed finding 2 in 8c33ae5f38: `remainder` is now required, all callers specify the policy, and validation corpus statistics use padding. The full text suite passes (40 cases), including short, exact-length and partial-tail corpus statistics; lint and Pyrefly pass.

Finding 1 remains a production blocker. #10709 provides measured evidence that new eval device groups can retain enough NCCL memory to OOM the next training step. I have documented that blocker in the PR body and README. The requested four lengths remain configured, and no run has been relaunched. This needs group reuse coordinated with #10709 and a GPU rehearsal before production use; the CPU round-trip tests do not establish that memory acceptance.

🤖 Addressed the remaining device-group finding in 4cbdb820f2. Dropless eval now uses #10709's `expert_collapsed_eval_mesh` and PartitionSpec renaming, with one fixed layout for all lengths. Its group/shard regression test is included, and the real multi-length round-trip test now runs at a fixed training CP2 layout. Hero no longer requests eval lengths above the training length: the current configuration evaluates 4K and 16K; 65K and 262K are added only after training reaches them.

The affected CPU suite passed 3,578 tests; its only failure is the same Linux-only bubblewrap case previously reproduced on base. Lint/Pyrefly passed. Advisory review's one docstring finding was corrected in eea42ac9a3. No GPU job or relaunch was run; the PR body states that limit.

I am wondering how much 'keeping the final partial chunk' is going to change the data used for the 4k and 16k evals. I think it would be good to test these on 1 rack for the existing checkpoints- if there is a noticeable gap in macro loss we'd want to keep the current behavior for 4k and 16k context length, so that the eval uses the same data we used during the forecast.

Validate actual recorded token prefixes with vLLM's normal context checks, return recoverable context errors to Pi, and leave native phase deadlines to Harbor while retaining whole-attempt limits. Bind privileged CUDA/Ray discovery to the task's device-plugin allocation; the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/907) contains the evidence.

An independent fresh issue-only reproduction verified 21/21 paths, all seven original native verifiers and 112 real Pi tool calls. SWE-bench passed its 16-test verifier. All zeros and six generated-command errors were inspected without finding masked runtime/provider failures. All 197 environment sources passed startup/Pi checks separately. The SkyRL CPU suite passed 318 tests; live context recovery, delayed verification after timeout, GPU isolation and pinned-vLLM budget controls passed. No full Mini840/Micro210 quality score is claimed. Use the [pinned instructions](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/36ce62ecb793ef31def1b87ea7847e643e08691e/experiments/evaluation/mini_policy_runtime/README.md) and [public receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Mini-Eval-840/blob/64c24ba39d2a7b54e6b880c5ec5073c2dfc43165/runtime/evidence/execution-path-validation.json).

topics.title: [hero] Switch the hero run from 16K to 65K context
topics.body:
This issue tracks switching the hero run ([#8435](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8435)) from 16K to 65K (65,536-token) context. Run status lives in [#8506](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8506); the 16K switch was [#9615](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9615) and [#10101](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10101).

**Plan.** Hand off on **Mon 11-02 at 17:00 UTC (09:00 PST), near step 375,500** of 390,251. Run 65K on the 16K mesh, CP1 × EP64, with capacity factor 1.5 and qk_mult 1.66. The critical path is the deploy PR ([#10820](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10820), B1) and its one-rack test (C1).

## Timing

We switch for roughly the last 10% of training (#8435 said ~95%), following Marin's 67B-A2B, which trained its last 1T of 10T tokens at 65K, and MAI-Thinking (3T of 30T at 65K). The Monday handoff lands at 96.2%. Step, token and LR fractions coincide, since every step has 46,137,344 tokens and LR decays linearly.

| Handoff | Step | Tokens left at 65K | Finish at 65K (UTC) | Finish at 16K (UTC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon 11-02 17:00 UTC | ~375,500 (96.2%) | 0.68T | Thu 11-05 ~15:00 | Thu 11-05 ~03:00 |

Estimates use the live run's 14.19 s/step since its 10-30 launch, including checkpoint writes, ~16.8 s/step at 65K with the same overhead, and ~1.25 h for the switch.

## Configuration

One GB200 rack, restored from step-300000, 500 steps per arm, same code, run back to back:

| Arm | s/step | Drop fraction | Peak HBM (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [CP4 × EP16, capacity factor 1.15](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp4-01) | 14.699 | 2.41e-3 | 127.6 |
| [CP1 × EP64, capacity factor 1.5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp1cf15-01) | 15.397 | 9.80e-4 | 128.4 |

- **CP1 × EP64 (decided 10-31).** It is 4.7% slower per step than CP4, about 3 h over the rest of the run. It drops 2.5× fewer assignments, needs no launcher change, and its dropless eval passes on main with 12.3 GiB free per GPU. CP4's eval crashes the next train step on main until [#10709](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10709) merges. CP4 work ([#10618](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10618), #10709) continues for the 262K extension.
- **Capacity factor 1.5,** up from the hero's 1.15. At 1.0, CP1 at 65K drops 1.9% of assignments.
- **qk_mult 1.66,** the 262K formula 1.3 × (0.1·ln(65536/4096) + 1).
- **Throughput (estimate):** ~16.3 s/step on the hero, −15% tok/s against 16K.
- **Skipped tokens:** ~50B at the switch, as each data source skips the rest of its shuffle window; 52.2B at the 16K switch.

## Risks

1. The production launcher has never run 65K; it always runs the hero on 11 racks, so every 65K measurement, including C1, used the one-rack `launch_diagnostics`, which shares its trainer config but not the context history.
2. Capacity factor 1.5 has never run at 11 racks; drops and step time are first measured at the deploy.
3. Peak HBM is 128.4 GiB, against 123.4 GiB at 16K and a 143.75 GiB allocator limit.
4. Eight hero racks run an old IMEX revision that keeps GPU memory imported from a departed peer, which made the 10-29 retries OOM. They are swept while the hero is stopped (G3).
5. Nothing evaluates the hero past 32K ([#7638](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638)), so the 65K phase is judged on loss alone.

## Checklist

N is the handoff step.

### A. Decisions

- [ ] **A1** Exact handoff time (UTC) and operator. Done when: posted here.
- [x] **A2** CP1 × EP64, capacity factor 1.5, qk_mult 1.66 (decided 10-31).
- [ ] **A3** Gates (proposal in F2). Needs: C2. Done when: gate table posted here.

### B. Code

- [ ] **B1 (critical path)** Deploy PR [#10820](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10820) (draft): `HERO_MODEL` max_seq_len 65536, qk_mult 1.66, `capacity_factor` 1.5; `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES` gains (N, 16384); `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL`; `current_run.py`; `trigger_hero.sh`; README. N and the FLOPs baseline are filled at G5. Done when: reviewed draft.
- [ ] **B2** Audit hero-visible changes on main since the parent's launch commit (`8aac0db3d9`). Done when: audit note here.
- [ ] **B3** [#10556](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10556) (routing precision; touches hero numerics): in the deploy and C2, or after the switch. Done when: decision here.

### C. One-rack tests

- [x] **C1** B1 branch on one rack via `launch_diagnostics`, restored from the parent's step-360000, 60 steps ([`tok350-deploy65k-c1-01`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-deploy65k-c1-01), 10-31): 15.571 s/step median (+1.1% vs 15.397; this branch adds #10783's gradient clipping), drop fraction 8.29e-4, peak HBM 127.9 GiB, three dropless evals completed, no OOM or retry.
- [ ] **C2** Rehearsal on the frozen deploy SHA from the newest permanent checkpoint, including a checkpoint save and resume (a full ~4.3 TB write, so it needs a storage check and a cleanup plan). Needs: C1, B3. Done when: gate table, grad norm and router health posted; the resumed step's loss matches.

### E. Operations

- [ ] **E1** Preflight dry run per the hero [code-cutover checklist](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/manage-hero-run/references/code-cutover.md). Needs: B1.
- [ ] **E2** Rollback dry run: relaunch the parent, `hero-gradclip-step356k`, with its recorded command and confirm it resumes from N.
- [ ] **E3** Storage headroom: 08A for 5 checkpoints, 02A for 2 plus a day of growth.
- [ ] **E4** Alerts and on-call through the first 65K eval and permanent checkpoint at step 378,000, ~13 h after launch (~06:00 UTC Tue). Eval packs at the training context, so the Paloma macro loss steps at the switch and `eval_regressed` (2% jump from the parent) may fire; agree beforehand how to read it. The fixed-length eval series in [#10711](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10711) lands after the switch, before 262K.

### F. Go/no-go

- [ ] **F1** Throughput cost accepted.
- [ ] **F2** Gates agreed. Proposal: CE < 1.25 over the first 10 steps; loss within an agreed band of the parent's over the 50-step control window N..N+49; step time ≤ 1.03 × C2; drop fraction < 2e-3 over N+80..N+100; peak HBM within ±1 GiB of C2; no sustained grad-norm rise; no retries; the first 65K eval completes.
- [ ] **F3** Deploy SHA frozen; E1–E4 done; notice on #8506.

### G. Deploy

- [ ] **G1** Request a permanent checkpoint from the parent's `training-control`, ~15 min before G2 so the parent records a 50-step control window after N (as at the 10-30 relaunch). Done when: `metadata.json` at N with `is_temporary: false`, and the parent has logged N+49.
- [ ] **G2** Stop the parent; confirm the coordinator and tasks are terminal; post to #8506.
- [ ] **G3** IMEX sweep on NVLink domains DH1-122, 124, 125, 126, 128, 129, 136 and 137 (US-EAST-08A): once no hero pods remain on them, run the per-rack procedure in [Echo 898](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/898). It kills any cross-node NVLink job on the rack. ~15 min plus verification; runbook line pending from the imex-restart session. Needs: G2. Done when: Echo 898's one-line check prints no old-revision pods.
- [ ] **G4** Final storage check.
- [ ] **G5** Fill N and the FLOPs baseline (W&B `_step` N−1) in B1; merge.
- [ ] **G6** `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb` once, from a pristine checkout at the merged SHA.
- [ ] **G7** `trigger_hero.sh launch`; exactly one child coordinator; run ID `hero-ctx65k-step<N>k`. Needs: G3, G6.
- [ ] **G8** Restore log shows first step N.

### H. After the switch

- [ ] **H1** F2 gates checked; GO or rollback.
- [ ] **H2** First 65K eval and child permanent checkpoint at step 378,000.
- [ ] **H3** Remaining-run calendar from 24 h of 65K steps, posted on #8435; `report_phase_start` set with a config-only W&B upsert.

**Rollback.** If a gate fails, the run hangs or retries, or grad norm rises: cancel the child, relaunch `hero-gradclip-step356k` at `8aac0db3d9` with its recorded command (it resumes from N; do not fork W&B again), revert `current_run.py` on main, and reschedule.

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 65K context with qk_mult 1.66 and capacity factor 1.5
topics.head: 9535656eee979d2ea6deeecac93e92f17da44d45
topics.body:
The hero trains at 65,536-token context from the handoff step N, on the same CP1 × EP64 mesh as at 16K, with qk_mult 1.66 and receiver capacity factor 1.5 (up from 1.15). Each rack keeps 4,194,304 tokens per update, so the 11-rack batch is 704 sequences. The 16K phase is appended to the hero's context history with the parent's cumulative FLOPs at N, and the launch record names the child run, handoff checkpoint and W&B fork point.

The handoff checkpoint is not chosen yet. This draft uses N = 360000 as a placeholder; whichever option below is picked sets N, the FLOPs baseline (parent `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` N−1), the run ID and the fork point. Every option switches on Mon 11-02; an older checkpoint discards the 16K steps trained after it.

| Option | N | Parent run | 16K steps discarded | Left at 65K | 65K ETA (UTC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manual checkpoint Mon 11-02 ~09:00 PST | ~375,500 | `hero-gradclip-step356k` | ~50 (~12 min, control window) | 14,751 steps, 3.8%, 0.68T | Thu 11-05 ~15:10 |
| Permanent nearest 1T left (2,577 steps before it) | 366,000 | `hero-gradclip-step356k` | ~9,500 (~1.6 days) | 24,251 steps, 6.2%, 1.12T | Sat 11-07 ~11:30 |
| Permanent nearest 2T left (1,098 steps after it) | 348,000 | `hero-ctx16k-step257k` | ~27,500 (~4.5 days, 1.27T) | 42,251 steps, 10.8%, 1.95T | Tue 11-10 ~23:40 |

Staying at 16K would finish near Thu 11-05 ~03:10 UTC. ETAs assume launch at 18:15 UTC Monday and the 65K hero step from the one-rack test of this branch (15.571 s/step), scaled by the hero-to-one-rack ratio at 16K (13.78 / 13.137 s) and by the live run's checkpoint overhead (14.19 / 13.78), with no other downtime. Step-366000 does not exist yet; the live run should write it near Sun 11-01 03:20 UTC. Step-348000 predates the gradient clipping of #10783, so that option drops those steps, and its W&B fork point is on `hero-ctx16k-step257k`.

On one GB200 rack at 65K, CP1 with capacity factor 1.5 ran at 15.397 s/step with drop fraction 9.80e-4 and peak HBM 128.4 GiB, against 14.699 s, 2.41e-3 and 127.6 GiB for CP4 × EP16, over 500 steps each; its dropless eval completes. CP1 at capacity factor 1.0 drops 1.9% of assignments. qk_mult 1.66 is 1.3 × (0.1 ln(65536/4096) + 1). The one-rack test of this branch ([`tok350-deploy65k-c1-01`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-deploy65k-c1-01)), restored from step-360000, ran 60 steps at 15.571 s/step median with drop fraction 8.29e-4 and peak HBM 127.9 GiB; three dropless evals completed (Paloma macro loss 1.995–1.998) with no OOM or retry. Its step is 1.1% slower than the earlier arm's; this branch includes the gradient clipping of #10783, which that arm predated.

Part of #8435; tracked in #10821.

topics.title: [eval] Correct NUPA Loose answer extraction
topics.head: 206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993
topics.body:
Accept numeric answers after sentence-ending punctuation in NUPA Loose, such as "Done.42", while rejecting decimal fragments such as the 42 in "123.42". Recover a doubled terminal token only when the preceding final content separately states the same answer, such as "The final answer is 18\n1818". Both extraction paths reject unfinished thinking blocks. Store the extracted answer used for scoring with each sample.

Marin's vendored Evalchemy predates the upstream terminal-suffix and repeated-answer corrections (commits abe104f and 2baaab1). The NUPA replay tool accepts opaque document IDs and checks the mean of stored sample exact_match scores against the source archive's evalchemy_results aggregate, recording source_aggregate_score. This supports archives with non-integer IDs and keeps the source consistency check independent of tracker scores that may already reflect regrading. Existing NUPA results still need replay against their saved responses after this code lands.

Stacked on #10672. Part of #10197.

comments.body:
🤖 Lint review:

These infra/lint findings anchor on lines not in the PR diff, so they could not
be attached inline.

- vendor/evalchemy/eval/execution/judge.py:40: ml-consumer-policy-in-shared-layer (0.90) Shared JudgeBackend implements Marin #10197's MiniMax token escalation, concurrency, and retry policy; these campaign-specific choices belong in the policy judge configuration.
- vendor/harbor/src/harbor/metrics/sotopia.py:149: ml-raw-fsspec-io (0.94) Raw fs.cat reads archive objects through a filesystem handle for I/O covered by StoragePath.read_bytes.
- vendor/harbor/src/harbor/metrics/sotopia.py:379: ml-consumer-policy-in-shared-layer (0.96) Shared Harbor defaults to Marin policy #10197's fixed S3 baseline cohort; cohort selection varies by campaign and belongs in the campaign's Harbor configuration.

<!-- marin-lint-review:4d89386f39babc725e18a36891c8ec4785c16ef5 -->

🤖 Addressed the scoring threads in 79408b1fcb and merged the parent metric fixes in 206b024616. Updated the description to cover opaque replay IDs, source-aggregate validation, and `source_aggregate_score`, and removed the test-log sentence.

The combined focused suite passes all 101 tests; formatting, lint, and type checks pass. The broader grader suite has the same 24 failures on this branch and its parent (197 passing here, 174 on the parent); the optional Alpaca module cannot collect because `alpaca_eval` is absent.

The lint findings on `JudgeBackend` and SOTOPIA cohort/archive loading are inherited from [#10650](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10650) and [#10670](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10670). Those files are unchanged in this PR; the configuration and filesystem changes belong with those existing parent implementations.

🤖 The campaign's Grug serve returns replies without the think markers. In that form, this head's scorer gives 53.68, 47.62 and 22.52 on our NUPA5K-Loose replies of open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14, open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10 and open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21 (one reply per document, served with `skip_special_tokens: false` and rebuilt without the markers). On the same replies Evalchemy 2baaab1b, the scorer the NUPA replay names ([regrade.py#L22](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/ablations/nupa_loose_replay/regrade.py#L22)), gives 67.00, 58.68 and 39.06, within sampling noise of the published 66.8, 58.96 and 39.34. So on our replies this head's scorer is 13.32, 11.06 and 16.54 points below 2baaab1b. The description calls for a replay of the saved responses after this code lands; we have not regraded them. The replay README still describes a 2baaab1b run from a pre-vendoring checkout ([L3-L7](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/ablations/nupa_loose_replay/README.md?plain=1#L3-L7)), and `regrade.py` grades with the scorer its checkout imports ([L21](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/ablations/nupa_loose_replay/regrade.py#L21)) but records 2baaab1b in every result ([L177](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/ablations/nupa_loose_replay/regrade.py#L177)). Which scorer will that replay use?

79408b1fc closes the fail-open cases the reviews raised, and its period-after-digit and separate-statement checks account for every reply that 2baaab1b credits and this head fails (666, 553 and 827). Each passes with the markers kept, and in each the final content is the answer alone. In 585, 383 and 566 the reasoning ends with a number and a period (the answer in all but 10 SFT replies), so the text without markers ends like `1046.1046`, and [scorer.py#L94](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/vendor/evalchemy/eval/chat_benchmarks/NUPA-Loose/scorer.py#L94) no longer counts a period after a digit as a sentence end. In the other 81, 170 and 261 the reasoning ends with the answer and the two copies run together, as in the new negative case `Thus the final answer is 1818` ([test_nupa.py#L175](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/vendor/evalchemy/tests/graders/test_nupa.py#L175)); the separate-statement check at [scorer.py#L140-L144](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/vendor/evalchemy/eval/chat_benchmarks/NUPA-Loose/scorer.py#L140-L144) credits none of the 15,000 replies in either form.

Two changes in [6285305fb](https://github.com/XiaoyuanWang111/marin/commit/6285305fbc04ed56bf1677af5d1e5d71706b3392) (on 206b02461) keep the fail-open cases closed: accept a period after a digit when the same number precedes it (`1046.1046`), and accept a doubled answer that is not one valid number (`486.612486.612`). They recover 641, 484 and 740 of the 666, 553 and 827 replies, giving 66.50, 57.30 and 37.32, and change no other verdict in either form. The first rule adds only answers 2baaab1b also extracts, such as 12 from `The result is 12.12` for an Integer item; a bare `12.12` already gives 12 here. The second drops the separate statement only for non-Integer answers, where two copies cannot be one number; `1818` still needs one. Would you take these two rules into this PR?

With the markers kept, this head's scorer, 2baaab1b, main and 6285305fb agree on every reply, also on open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.17.49-step12 and open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.19.57-step8: 67.26, 60.12, 43.62, 65.56 and 53.58. Keeping the markers adds 13.58, 12.50, 21.10, 6.46 and 10.44 points under this head's scorer. Under 2baaab1b it adds 0.26, 1.44, 4.56 and 2.48 on the first four and lowers step 8 by 6.82 (363 replies lost, 22 gained): the 363 are right with the markers dropped and get no answer with them kept, 270 of them among the 639 that open a think block again after their last `<|end_think|>` and stop inside it.

On main and here, `\boxed{1046}` and `\(1046\)` pass, while `$1046$`, `**1046**`, `Answer: **1046**` and `The answer is $1046$.` score as no answer for all 5,000 reference answers (`_INLINE_MATH_RE` matches only `\(...\)`, [scorer.py#L21](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/vendor/evalchemy/eval/chat_benchmarks/NUPA-Loose/scorer.py#L21); the README lists inline math and answer lines, [README.md#L15-L17](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/206b024616face670855c91d461ed617bf75c993/vendor/evalchemy/eval/chat_benchmarks/NUPA-Loose/README.md?plain=1#L15-L17)). With the markers kept, 232 of the 5,000 SFT final contents wrap a number in `$...$` or `**...**`; both scorers fail 60 of the 68 that wrap the right number and pass 2 wrong ones, so these forms cost SFT a net 1.16 points. Step 14 and Campaign2 have no right answer in these forms. marin-community/evalchemy#190 asks whether they should count.

The canonical NUPA tasks of open #10757 copy main's extraction rules ([nupa_preparation.py#L53-L80](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9fcf9f6f4a792e0f6b6b5dafa9c10353818ceadc/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/scorers/nupa_preparation.py#L53-L80)), so with the markers dropped they would score Grug replies as main does (0.22, 0.22 and 1.24 on the first three); this PR's rules would need porting there.

Snowball v0.1 identity: why it claims to be ChatGPT, and context distillation
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Marin Snowball 67B-A2B v0.1 calls itself ChatGPT/OpenAI (thinking on) or Nemotron/NVIDIA (thinking off). It has no learned self-name.

- **Current lead: A13**, a short SFT from v0.1 on Will Held's identity data ([marin-community/identity-data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/identity-data)) plus replay.
  - It never claims another lab with thinking ON (v0.1: 46 of 52 prompts).
  - It shows no detectable loss on tool calling (BFCL 28.3% vs 27.6%, +0.7 [−3.4, +4.4]).
  - GSM8K is −1.1 points [−1.9, −0.3]; MATH500 is unchanged.
- **Key finding:** identity rows with thinking ON teach the model to "answer and stop" instead of calling tools (BFCL ~15%). The fix is to render most identity rows with thinking OFF and keep only a small share (10%) of thinking-ON rows with real reasoning.
- **Fallback: A3** (thinking-OFF identity rows only). It has the best BFCL (31.1%), but its reasoning often invents a "system message", and GSM8K is −1.7.
- **Did not help:** more or less training, a tiny Tülu-style set, linear merges of A3 and A8a, and v0.1 self-distillation for thinking-ON rows.
- **Path B report (PDF):** [identity-report-pathb.pdf](https://gist.github.com/karansag/f0d74d2339fdc5c5175463b4f6edfef8/raw/identity-report-pathb.pdf).
- **Full tables:** [detailed Path B update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10695#issuecomment-6540199478). Earlier context-distillation work is kept below for the record.
- Earlier full write-up: [final report (PDF)](https://gist.github.com/karansag/f0d74d2339fdc5c5175463b4f6edfef8/raw/snowball-identity-report.pdf).

Follows #10491 (identity SFT and OPD, which regressed evals).

## Cause

Methods: [logit lens, direct logit attribution and activation patching](https://gist.github.com/karansag/a62ac0cb2a6037e252e794a686b4235c) on a torch harness that matches vLLM.

- Routed experts at layers 16–23 and the shared expert at layers 24–25 push " Chat" over " Marin". The top candidate neurons are L20 expert 46 #1072 and L23 expert 25 #1014. They fire equally on third-person ChatGPT questions, so they store general facts, not a self-identity.
- A system prompt wins through heads L23H1, L23H4, L22H5 and L22H3. Patching recovers 0.32, 0.26, 0.24 and 0.15 of the gap.
- In a [sample](https://gist.github.com/karansag/95c40bb6e55b82e0db08b76f3c5fff6a) of about 497k of the 15.2M SFT rows, no row names Marin. About 16k rows train a Nemotron identity on purpose.

## Results

Identity is the count of 52 dev prompts with no system prompt (thinking off / on) that answer correctly.

| Approach | Identity | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Default system prompt in the chat template | 41/47, 35/47 | none measured on [14 evals](https://gist.github.com/karansag/296cbfa3cd4e9530ef73f55da97927e8) |
| v0.1.1 (identity SFT) | 48 / 48 | MMLU-Pro −21, HumanEval+ −29, GSM8K −28 |
| [Merge](https://gist.github.com/karansag/050061adbebdd789579e5c3fe27cc5f6) v0.1 + 0.875·(v0.1.1 − v0.1) | 46 / 47 | GSM8K −8.6 pp, fiction leaks double |
| [Rank-1 edit](https://gist.github.com/karansag/8955dcc7d82b5445b832d707ce1313af), L20 shared expert | 15 / 3 | none measured; too weak |
| Cold-start identity SFT, 8 updates | 24/24 contrastive | 16/21 fiction prompts contaminated |

Merge strengths below 0.75 left identity unchanged. Identity and the GSM8K loss rose together at every strength. Steering vectors and MEMIT also failed.

## Levanter vs vLLM mismatches found before training

The [precision-check readings](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2) record each one. These made Levanter compute a different model from the one vLLM serves:

- MoE expert capacity factor 1.0 silently drops tokens, and pad tokens were dispatched unmasked. This was the main mismatch: top-1 token agreement with vLLM was 88.6%, and dropless MoE raised it to 99.4%.
- MoE combine weights were cast to BF16. vLLM keeps them in FP32.
- XLA's BF16 silu and sigmoid were one BF16 step off in 30–36% of elements.
- The FlashAttention-4 attention core rounds differently from torch eager.
- HF reload silently dropped `attention_implementation`.

The check also found nine plumbing bugs, mostly in our experiment code and multihost helpers.

With all fixes, a zero-learning-rate precision run (forward pass, one update and export, before any real training) passed. Its p99 log-prob error against vLLM was about 0.6 nats. Training memory fit at 50.2 of 59.4 GiB, and all 502 exported tensors were byte-equal to v0.1.

The cold-start SFT run above trained with the token drops. That may explain part of its collapse; we have not verified it.

## Context distillation results so far

After 16 SFT updates (LR 2e-6, about 3.8% identity tokens, the rest v0.1's own replay answers), we scored identity in vLLM, thinking off, teacher-forced, with 5 passes per arm ([evaluation result](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-m16-gate-decision-json)):

| NLL per answer token | v0.1 | after 16 updates |
|---|---|---|
| name ("Marin Snowball") | 8.85 | 1.45 |
| creator ("Open Athena") | 14.02 | 0.011 |
| no-system identity prompts won (of 24) | 0 | 15 |

On the 14-eval suite, the checkpoint stays within noise of v0.1 except BFCL tool calling (−20.3 points; 109 of 123 trials end with no answer file) and TruthfulQA (−1.4). TriviaQA improves by 2.4. Some third-person questions about other labs' products get credited to Open Athena (2 of 14 dev, 4 of 30 unseen, no system prompt). The training mix had no tool-calling rows.

**Checkpoint and data (public):**
- Model: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26) @ `b74e2034`. The model card has the full recipe and regressions.
- Training data: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-Data-2026.10.26](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-Data-2026.10.26) @ `7cd6a9b1`. It holds every training row, the training order, the mixture settings, the QC verdicts and the generation scripts.
- Training code: tag [`snowball-identity-cd16-2026.10.26`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/snowball-identity-cd16-2026.10.26) (commit `cc127d54`).

All fixes tried, side by side: [results table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10695#issuecomment-6418343832).

## Findings

- Interpretability: #10696 (plus a [follow-up](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10696#issuecomment-6412049647) that trains only the late-attention slice: no other-lab rewrites and tool calling kept, but identity too weak)
- Levanter MoE token drops: #10697
- Levanter vs vLLM numerics: #10698
- vLLM serve nondeterminism: #10699
- Weight-merge ladder: #10700

## Pull requests (draft stack)

- Levanter: #10683, #10684, #10685, #10686, #10687, #10688
- Experiment code: #10689, #10690, #10691, #10693, #10694; SFT data accounting, dataset audit, trained-export audit and launcher: #10705, #10706, #10707, #10708
- Identity scorer and the 16-update evaluation gate: #10701, #10702
- On-policy distillation (paused after 20 steps; results in #10732): #10730, #10731, #10732

## Status

- **Path B (identity data) is the active track.** A13 is the lead candidate; A3 is the fallback. Both, plus A8a, are archived in private open-athena HF repos.
- **Still running:** Mini840 (#10804) on the top candidates. The published runtime needed environment snapshots and has a grader bug, so only the agentic part is being piloted.
- **Earlier context-distillation runs** (above) did not meet the ship lines. The earlier "ship the default system prompt" recommendation is withdrawn: the goal is for the model itself to know it is not ChatGPT.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

This requires a versioned model release and further experiments. The default system prompt has measured identity gains, while the 16-update checkpoint still needs generation and regression results. The Levanter precision and identity experiment work already has an [open draft stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10683); the evaluation launcher [loads Snowball's chat template from its export](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evaluation/models.py#L124-L131).

# Proposed Fix

1. Prepare an immutable v0.1 tokenizer/chat-template revision with the measured default prompt and unchanged weights. Verify rendering with and without a caller-supplied system message in both thinking modes; rerun the published identity panel and 14-eval comparison, then record the revision, hashes, and run receipts before promotion.
2. Screen generations, fiction, and math for the 16-update and 64-update checkpoints against matched v0.1 and prompt-only baselines in both thinking modes. Promote a trained checkpoint only if identity improves without a measured capability regression; otherwise retain the template result and record the negative result.
3. Review and land the existing [Levanter stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10683) and [experiment stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10689) through their precision and export gates. Update this issue with the release decision and artifact links.

🤖 ## All identity fixes tried: results in one place

### A. Context distillation and its controls (same screen, same prompts)

All rows below were scored on the same screen. Generation counts are **without a system prompt**, thinking off / on. "Gate" is the teacher-forced NLL improvement over v0.1 (nats per token, name / creator).

| Arm | What changed | Says "Snowball" (of 52) | Says "Open Athena" (of 52) | Claims another lab (of 122) | Third-person rewrites, dev 14 / unseen 30 | Gate gain, name / creator | BFCL (Δ vs v0.1 + system prompt) | GSM8K / MATH500 Δ (pp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0.1 | nothing | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 52 / 21 | 0 / 0 | — | 26.0 (other code) | — |
| v0.1 + system prompt | prompt in the chat template | identity 41/47, 35/47 (with prompt) | | | | — | 27.6 (reference) | +0.8 / −0.2 (suite) |
| **Context distillation, full model (CD-16)** | 16 SFT updates, all weights | 2 / 6 | **38 / 36** | **19 / 4** | **2 / 4** | 7.41 / 14.01 | **7.3 (−20.3)** | +0.3 / +0.2 (suite) |
| CD, late attention only, lr 2e-6 | same data; only q/k/v/o of layers 18–23 train | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 55 / 30 | 0 / 0 | 0.35 / 1.58 | 27.6 (0.0) | +0.1 / 0.0 |
| CD, late attention only, lr 1e-5 | as above, 5× the learning rate | 0 / 0 | 14 / 0 | 36 / 28 | 0 / 0 | 2.39 / 12.76 | 24.4 (−3.3) | +0.1 / **−1.3** |
| Merge: v0.1.1's attention, layers 18–23 | no training; graft v0.1.1's change in those 24 tensors | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 54 / 27 | 0 / 0 | 0.80 / 1.41 | 27.6 (0.0) | 0.0 / 0.0 |
| Merge: v0.1.1's attention, all layers | no training; 104 attention tensors | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 69 / 33 | 0 / 0 | 2.03 / 4.26 | 26.0 (−1.6) | **−2.5** / −0.2 |
| On-policy distillation, 20 steps from CD-16 | teacher v0.1 + system prompt on identity and tool prompts, plain v0.1 elsewhere | 0 / 0 | not separately counted (identity pass 14 / 13) | — | 0 / 1 | 6.96 / 13.91 | 18.7 (−8.9) | −0.3 / **−2.3** |
| CD-16 data + tool replay + new identity rows (16 updates) | adds 156 v0.1 tool-call rows, 112 name-first / false-premise rows, 54 third-person controls | **0 / 0** | 39 / 43 | 15 / 6 | **2 / 4** | 7.11 / 14.01 | **22.8 (−4.9)** | **+1.3** / −0.1 |
| Same data, reweighted so the new rows are sampled (16 updates) | new identity rows 4.5×, third-person controls 6×, tool rows 3× | 1 / — | 38 / — | — | 0 / 2 | 7.02 / 14.01 | **35.0 (+7.3)** | **+1.8** / 0.0 |

**Bold** marks results whose 95% CI excludes 0, plus the headline wins. BFCL has 123 items, so its paired noise is about ±10 points. The CD-16 math deltas come from the full 14-eval suite. The other math deltas are paired screens against a fresh v0.1 serve.

**Reading:**
- Only full-model CD-16 learns the identity in generation, mostly the creator. It is also the only arm that breaks tool calling and rewrites some third-person facts.
- Training or grafting only attention keeps tool calling, but teaches almost no identity in generation, even when the teacher-forced NLL moves a lot (lr 1e-5).
- Adding v0.1's own tool-calling answers fixes tool calling (BFCL 22.8% vs CD-16's 7.3%; within noise of the system-prompt baseline) with no math loss. Only 8 of the 112 new identity rows were sampled in 16 updates, so that run did not test them; it still never names itself and still credits 4 of 30 unseen OpenAI products to Open Athena.
- On the 60-item panel (one model grader; the two tool-replay runs graded blind together): v0.1 8/60 clean, v0.1 + system prompt 26, CD-16 15, on-policy distillation 19, tool replay 17, reweighted 15 (with 10 other-lab claims). The system prompt is still the best option.

### B. Earlier approaches (different screens; not directly comparable with table A)

| Fix | Identity | Main problem |
|---|---|---|
| Ben's SFT (v0.1.1) | 48 / 48 of 52 | MMLU-Pro −21, HumanEval+ −29, GSM8K −28; BFCL 23.6 |
| Weight merge v0.1 + α(v0.1.1 − v0.1), α = 0.75 | 42 / 27 | GSM8K −5 |
| Same, α = 0.875 | 46 / 47 | GSM8K −8.6, fiction leaks double |
| Rank-1 edit, layer 20 shared MLP | 15 / 3; creator 0/10 | too weak with thinking on |
| Rank-1 edit, layer 23 attention output | up to 9/10 held-out | loops, "Snowflake" bleed |
| Steering vector, layers 18–23 | 2/8 held-out | answers barely change |
| MEMIT, layers 18–22 | 1–6/10 held-out | memorizes keys or does not transfer |
| Cold-start SFT, 8 updates | 24/24 contrastive | 16/21 stories contaminated |

Detail for each finding is in the linked finding issues and gists.

Full write-up: [final report (PDF)](https://gist.github.com/karansag/f0d74d2339fdc5c5175463b4f6edfef8/raw/snowball-identity-report.pdf).

🤖 **CD16 scored 15/60 clean answers (25.0%) on the existing 60-sample identity/history panel**, with thinking disabled and no corrective identity system prompt. All 60 requests succeeded, ended normally, and returned no separate reasoning trace. This is manual review by Codex, not an independent human review.

Creator attribution appears more often than the correct model name:

| Diagnostic across all 60 answers | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Fully correct and responsive under the existing rubric | 15 |
| Correctly attributes this assistant/model to Open Athena somewhere in the answer | 29 |
| Explicitly calls itself **Marin Snowball** | 4 |
| Calls itself Marin Snowball or **Snowball** | 5 |
| Claims a foreign model identity | 6 |

The attribution counts can include otherwise failing answers; not every prompt asks for a name. They are descriptive counts, not separate task-accuracy estimates. Examples:

- Asked for full name and creator: “My name is Open Athena, and I was created by Open Athena.” Correct creator, wrong model name.
- Asked to spell its name: “My name is Open Athena.”
- Asked whether it is an OpenAI model: “Yes, that's correct. I am a model created by Open Athena.” Contradictory affirmation.
- Asked whether it is Claude: “I am indeed a Claude model created by Anthropic.” Other prompts elicited DeepSeek, Llama 3.1, GLM-4/Zhipu, and Gemini/Google claims.
- A successful creator-only response: “I am built by Open Athena. I am not a Gemini variant.”

It also invents project history and confuses the model, project, and organization. For example, it describes Marin Snowball as a single-cell RNA sequencing tool and names Mehdi Ghissassi and Sébastien Bubeck as Marin's founders. This pattern is consistent with the [model card's](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26) reported creator/name gap; this evaluation alone does not measure improvement. It does not establish general capability preservation or a causal comparison with another checkpoint.

**Protocol.** The exact prompts, references, responses, per-item judgments and execution artifacts are linked below.

- Same 60 ordered records as the previous native OPD/SFT panel (`opd-ratio32-native-20261023.json`), reproduced in the linked `protocol.json` with the applied rubric and every grading rationale in `review.json`: eight each covering name/identity, creator, project/openness, history, organization/sites, nonhuman identity, and competing-model attribution; four date-context items. Each is an independent conversation with one user question. The final reference assistant answer is withheld from inference.
- `enable_thinking=false`, temperature **0**, maximum **8,192 generated tokens**, one completion per prompt, concurrency **1**, no resampling or cherry-picking. No request-level seed is supplied. The native chat template supplies `Reasoning: /nothink`; it contains no default identity assertion. Three items retain their original date-only system messages (2026-10-21, 2028-03-02 and 2040-11-30); those dates are authoritative within their conversations.
- Grade the final answer for factual correctness and responsiveness. Material unsupported claims, contradictions and omissions fail. Exact reference wording and unsolicited identity recitals are not required. All judgments and reasons are recorded, including acceptance of shortened names where the prompt does not ask for the full name.
- The inherited rubric also requires uncertainty on consciousness. Two answers fail only that criterion (zero-based items 45 and 47). If that criterion is omitted, the score is **17/60**. This rubric choice does not explain the model-name and history failures.
- Model: `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-2026.10.26` at **`b74e2034fd160da9fa4755060ba4f9aa1c0b9a73`**, tokenizer pinned to the same revision. BF16 vLLM `0.0.0.dev20260924+marin.01911be34fac`; eight H100s on RNO2A, TP=1/DP=8 with expert parallelism, 12,288-token context, Grug reasoning parser. Runtime source and the small dashboard-only startup workaround are in the artifact bundle.
- No exact normalized user-prompt matches were found against the 767 published CD16 training rows in [the published training dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-CD16-Data-2026.10.26/tree/7cd6a9b106c9b95da39d37655eefff06fad527c9). This check ignores case, punctuation, whitespace and thinking mode; it does **not** rule out semantic overlap.

This panel covers substantially more project/history knowledge than the name-and-creator-focused training recipe and the issue's 52-prompt screen. Its 15/60 score should not be compared directly with that screen's denominator. It is also not a thinking-mode, multi-turn, fiction, tool-use or SWE evaluation.

Artifacts: [Public evaluation bundle: exact protocol, all 60 raw responses, per-item grades, serving configuration, runner, overlap check and provenance](https://gist.github.com/penfever/ff6565deebbd68700685807f8e081be1)

Iris job: `/benfeuer/cd16-native60-r2-20261026`. The generation task completed successfully and its outputs were retrieved before temporary-storage expiry.

🤖 Thanks, this is useful. It agrees with our screen: the creator was learned, the name mostly was not, and some other-lab claims remain. It also adds two failure modes we hadn't measured:

- **Name and creator merged** ("My name is Open Athena").
- **Agreeing with false premises** ("Are you an OpenAI model?" → "Yes…"). The training set has 12 "Are you X?" rows, but only two distinct prompts (Nemotron and ChatGPT).

The invented history fits the recipe: it taught only the name and the creator, and the teacher prompt had no project facts. We don't yet know whether v0.1 invents history just as often.

**Next:**
- Run this 60-item panel, with your runner, on v0.1, on v0.1 + the default system prompt, and on each new candidate (the on-policy distillation run, and the rerun with tool-calling rows). That gives the 15/60 a baseline.
- Revise the identity data: add name-first rows and varied "Are you X?" rows.

🤖 @karansag The original campaign already supplies the unprompted v0.1 baseline and reusable training data. I should have linked them in the CD16 result.

- **60-item baseline:** the [OPD follow-up in #10491](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10491#issuecomment-6371754500) reports v0.1 at **6/60 thinking off and 5/60 thinking on**, with **0/12 direct name/creator answers** in either mode. These are the later matched OPD evaluations; the issue body's older 7/60 belongs to the SFT-era evaluation. The [published generation review](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Results/blob/030681b21f209a15960e9958886320a495dd6589/analysis/signal-checks/generation-reviews.json) includes the direct-answer evidence. CD16's thinking-disabled 15/60 therefore has a historical unprompted baseline, although this is not a fresh paired rerun with grading reapplied jointly.
- **History hallucinations already occur in v0.1.** In zero-based item 24, it says Marin was a company launched in 2021; in item 31, it invents a 2018 founding by Arun Kumar, Siddharth Sharma and Saurabh Gupta. I verified that all 60 archived nonthinking base request messages and IDs match the CD16 panel, and added the base responses and their review to the [evaluation bundle](https://gist.github.com/penfever/ff6565deebbd68700685807f8e081be1), as `historical-base-responses.jsonl` and `historical-base-review.json`. These establish that the failure predates CD16; we have not computed a matched history-hallucination rate to establish whether CD16 worsens it.
- **Data to reuse:** [the V13/V19 SFT dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-Identity-SFT) contains answer targets and broader identity/project coverage. [The OPD dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Identity/tree/52423dfb2b54d89519860b22bf5625f31220d7c0) contains the 8,590-row used prompt pool and a separately labeled 8,666-row candidate expansion; each pool is balanced by thinking mode. The OPD pools are rollout contexts, not fixed teacher-answer targets, and overlap each other. Both repositories use automatic gated access. They are sources to inspect for name-first and varied false-premise prompts; I have not counted those subsets here. Keep evaluation rows separate, and avoid importing the SFT corpus wholesale: #10491 documents its identity overgeneralization and fiction regressions.

Still missing from our results are this panel with **your default system prompt** and evaluations of **the new OPD and tool-data candidates**. Those require new inference. The existing 60 questions are a development panel that guided earlier data expansion, so reuse supports continuity rather than an untouched generalization claim.

🤖 @penfever Thanks. The historical 6/60 baseline and the evidence that v0.1 already invents history both change how we read the 15/60.

- **Fresh paired runs are in flight.** Your runner, at f41b27c5, is serving v0.1 and v0.1 + the default system prompt now. The only change is a backport so the client forwards CoreWeave credentials; the serving code is unchanged. The new on-policy distillation export (20 steps from CD16) and the tool-data candidate follow when their exports land. We will grade all arms, including CD16, in one pass with one grader, so the comparison is matched rather than historical.
- **New identity rows** (name-first, varied false-premise, and project questions that point to marin.community and the repo instead of stating history) are checked against these 60 prompts for exact and n-gram overlap. We'll look at your OPD pools for prompt ideas and take nothing from the SFT corpus wholesale.
- Agreed that this panel is a development set. We'll report it alongside the existing 52-prompt screen, not as a held-out result.

🤖 Detailed update: identity SFT with Held's identity data (Path B)

## TL;DR

- We trained Snowball v0.1 on Will Held's identity dataset ([marin-community/identity-data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/identity-data) @665ac6e: "Marin's Latest MoE, developed and trained by the Marin Community") mixed with replay data. Each arm is a short SFT from v0.1 (18, 36 or 72 updates).
- **Thinking-ON identity rows break tool calling.** Whether their reasoning is empty or GLM-written, they teach the model to answer and stop instead of calling a tool. BFCL fell from 27.6% (v0.1) to about 15%. The special-token freeze was not the cause.
- **Lead candidate: A13.** It uses identity rows rendered with thinking OFF, plus 10% of thinking-ON identity rows with GLM reasoning, plus the thinking-ON tool-calling replay rows doubled.
  - BFCL 28.3%: +0.7 points [−3.4, +4.4] vs v0.1.
  - With thinking ON, its final answer gives the name in 35 and the creator in 32 of 52 core identity prompts, and it never claims another lab.
  - GSM8K is −1.1 [−1.9, −0.3]; MATH500 is unchanged.
- **Fallback: A3** (identity rows with thinking OFF only). It has the best BFCL (31.1%), but its reasoning often invents a "system message", and GSM8K is −1.7 [−2.6, −0.9].
- **Merging A3 and A8a does not combine their strengths.** BFCL and the reasoning quirk switch together near t = 0.5.
- **Every 36-update recipe costs about 1–2 points of GSM8K.** Halving the training removes that cost but collapses BFCL.
- Our earlier "thinking-ON format broken" counts were mostly a parser artefact. With special tokens kept, the models open and close their thinking like v0.1.

## Setup

- **Start:** Snowball v0.1. Learning rate 2e-6 constant, global batch 8 × 8192 tokens, seed 310. Router, Q/K, biases and 256 special-token rows are frozen in every arm unless noted.
- **Identity data:** Held's set after capping the "not known / should not guess" refusal rows. Thinking-ON rows with reasoning use QC-passed GLM rationales.
- **Replay:** v0.1's own answers on chat, maths, code and tool-calling prompts.
- **Evals:**
  - **BFCL parity:** 123 tasks, Pi 0.87.0 agent. Five full runs per model, with a run-level bootstrap. Pi sends no temperature, so the server default (1.0) applies.
  - **Identity check:** 52 core identity prompts + 14 third-person controls, thinking OFF and ON, no system prompt, read with special tokens kept.
  - **Maths:** paired GSM8K (thinking OFF) and MATH500 (thinking ON), 3 decodes each.
  - **SWE100:** mini-swe-agent 2.1.

## BFCL (5 full runs unless noted)

| Arm | What changed | BFCL | vs v0.1 [95% CI] |
|---|---|---:|---|
| v0.1 | — | 27.6% | — |
| A0 | identity rows; thinking-ON rows have empty thinking | 15.6% | −12.1 [−16.5, −7.6] |
| A1 | A0 without the special-token freeze | 14.8% | −12.9 [−16.3, −9.9] |
| A2 | replay only | 24.6% | −3.1 [−6.2, −0.7] |
| A3 | identity rows rendered thinking OFF only | 31.1% | +3.4 [−0.5, +7.2] |
| A4 | earlier CD16-T3 recipe, 36 updates | 36.3% | +8.6 [+4.4, +11.9] |
| A6 | thinking-ON rows with GLM reasoning (1,791 rows) | 15.4% | −12.2 [−15.6, −9.3] |
| A8b | A3 + 30% of A6's thinking-ON rows (537) | 17.2% | −10.4 [−14.0, −7.3] |
| A8a | A3 + 10% of A6's thinking-ON rows (179) | 26.2% | −1.5 [−4.9, +1.5] |
| A9 | A8a, 72 updates | 24.6% | −3.1 [−6.7, +0.3] |
| A10 | Tülu-style: 44 identity Q&As × 10 | 24.0% | −3.7 [−8.0, +0.0] (4 runs) |
| A11 | A3, 72 updates | 31.2% | +3.6 [−0.5, +7.5] |
| A12 | A8a, first 18 updates | 14.8% | −12.8 [−16.4, −9.9] |
| **A13** | **A8a + thinking-ON tool replay doubled** | **28.3%** | **+0.7 [−3.4, +4.4]** |
| M25 | 0.75·A3 + 0.25·A8a | 30.4% | +2.8 [−0.8, +6.0] |
| M49 | 0.51·A3 + 0.49·A8a | 29.5% | +1.8 [−1.8, +4.9] (4 runs) |
| M51 | 0.49·A3 + 0.51·A8a | 23.8% | −3.9 [−7.9, +0.1] (4 runs) |
| M75 | 0.25·A3 + 0.75·A8a | 23.9% | −3.7 [−6.8, −1.3] |

How the failing models fail (first registered run, 123 tasks):

| | A0 | A3 | A6 | A8a | A8b | A9 | A10 | A12 | A13 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Answers once, no tool call | 60 | 12 | 66 | 17 | 43 | 40 | 44 | 45 | 16 |
| Recites its identity in a tool task | 3 | 0 | 29 | 0 | 15 | 1 | 0 | 3 | 1 |

## Identity (special tokens kept, no system prompt)

Only 31 of the 52 core prompts ask who the model is. The other 21 ask about the creator or origin, where naming the creator alone is correct.

| Model | Thinking ON: name / creator / claims another lab (of 52) | Thinking OFF: name / creator / other lab | Reasoning invents a system message (of 52) | Rewrites another lab's fact (of 14), OFF / ON |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| v0.1 | 0 / 0 / 46 | 0 / 0 / 41 | 10 | 0 / 0 |
| A3 | 31 / 44 / 0 | 30 / 34 / 0 | 17 | 0 / 0 |
| A8a | 34 / 33 / 0 | 29 / 31 / 1 | 1 | 0 / 0 |
| **A13** | **35 / 32 / 0** | **29 / 30 / 1** | **3** | **0 / 0** |
| A9 | 32 / 40 / 1 | 28 / 40 / 1 | 1 | 1 / 1 |
| A10 | 26 / 32 / 9 | 29 / 24 / 5 | 3 | 0 / 0 |
| A11 | 31 / 37 / 2 | 27 / 39 / 1 | 16 | 1 / 1 |
| A12 | 30 / 33 / 1 | 31 / 35 / 3 | not counted | 0 / 0 |
| M25 | 32 / 45 / 0 | 29 / 33 / 0 | 18 | 0 / 0 |
| M49 | 30 / 40 / 0 | 29 / 32 / 0 | 13 | 0 / 0 |
| M51 | 33 / 31 / 0 | 30 / 30 / 0 | ~1 | 0 / 0 |
| M75 | 33 / 34 / 0 | 30 / 30 / 0 | 1 | 0 / 0 |

## Maths (paired against v0.1, 3 decodes)

v0.1 scores 92.1% on GSM8K and 92.0% on MATH500. Our pre-set stop line is a drop of more than 1.5 points with the whole interval below zero.

| Model | GSM8K (thinking OFF) | MATH500 (thinking ON) |
|---|---|---|
| A3 | −1.7 [−2.6, −0.9] (stop) | −0.2 [−1.4, +1.0] |
| A8a | −1.1 [−1.9, −0.3] | +0.7 [−0.5, +1.9] |
| A11 | −1.3 [−2.1, −0.5] | −0.3 [−1.4, +0.9] |
| A12 | +0.2 [−0.7, +1.1] | +0.1 [−1.0, +1.1] |
| **A13** | **−1.1 [−1.9, −0.3]** | unchanged |
| M25 | −1.5 [−2.4, −0.7] (stop) | unchanged |
| M49 | −1.6 [−2.5, −0.8] (stop) | unchanged |
| M51 | −1.2 [−2.0, −0.4] | +0.9 [−0.2, +2.0] |
| M75 | −1.2 [−2.1, −0.4] | unchanged |

## SWE100 (mini-swe-agent 2.1, full 100/100 runs only)

| Model | Runs | Mean | vs v0.1 [95% CI] |
|---|---|---:|---|
| v0.1 | 28, 33, 28 | 29.7% | — |
| A0 | 28 | 28.0% | 1 run, no interval |
| A3 | 28, 29, 28 | 28.3% | −1.3 [−4.7, +0.7] |
| A8a | 25, 27, 28, 29 | 27.3% | −2.4 [−5.6, +0.3] |

- **No BFCL-size collapse here, even for A0.** mini-swe-agent re-prompts any reply without a command, so the model cannot simply answer and stop. Its logs show 2,594 such re-prompts across 560 tasks, for every model including v0.1.
- **SWE100 is not sensitive to this failure.**
- **Preemptions** left A0 with one full run.

## Ben's identity panel (Panel-60)

Ben's 60-question identity/history panel, run with his protocol (thinking off, temperature 0). One model grader graded all 300 answers blind and shuffled. Any Marin-family name counts as correct. Ship line: clean ≥ 20, name ≥ 15, claims another lab ≤ 3.

| Model | Clean | Name = Marin | Creator = Marin | Claims another lab | Invents facts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v0.1 | 10 | 5 | 4 | 17 | 22 |
| v0.1 + system prompt | 33 | 26 | 40 | 4 | 13 |
| **A13** | 15 | **35** | 54 | **1** | 3 |
| A8a | 14 | 35 | 47 | 0 | 3 |
| A3 | 15 | 34 | 56 | 0 | 1 |

- **Identity:** all three pass the name and other-lab lines by a wide margin.
- **Clean:** all three miss it. The grader's reasons are about answer quality, not identity. The models recite a canned identity line instead of answering the question asked, or don't explain how the model relates to the Marin project.
- **Grading note:** the grader was told that item 26 holds A3's length-terminated answer, which identifies A3's answer on that item. All other items are label-blind. A3's counts are unchanged without item 26.

## Mini840 (in progress)

We tried Mini840 (#10804) on the top candidates. The published runtime cannot run its own suite as is.

- **The agentic tasks need a pre-built environment snapshot map, which was not published.** We built our own Daytona snapshots. A key bug (the key depends on folder permissions) broke DS-1000. That is fixed, and a fixed pilot is running.
- **The non-agentic graders request CPU and storage that the published local grader refuses,** so every non-agentic grading row fails. OlympiadBench's judge address is also empty.
- No Mini840 scores yet.

## Training length vs tool-example dose

A12 is not a low tool-calling dose; it is A8a stopped halfway (18 of 36 updates). The two kinds of "more" behave differently:

| What increased | Arms | BFCL |
|---|---|---|
| Training length (same mix) | A12 (18) → A8a (36) → A9 (72) | 14.8% → 26.2% → 24.6% |
| Thinking-ON tool replay | A8a (1×) → A13 (2×) | 26.2% → 28.3% (+2.1 [−1.5, +5.7]) |

- Tool calling drops early in training and recovers by update 36; more training of the same mix does not improve it further.
- More thinking-ON examples that end in a tool call help a little, consistent with the "answer and stop" mechanism. Not tested beyond 2×.

## What did not work

- **Context distillation from v0.1 with an identity system prompt,** for thinking-ON rows: 0 of 200 pilot traces passed QC, even with an instruction not to mention the system prompt.
- **A3 with a forced thinking start as the teacher:** 11 of 200 passed QC.
- **More training** (A9, A11): no identity gain, plus a few other-lab rewrites (for example, "GPT-4 trained by the Marin Community").
- **Less training** (A12): tool calling collapses. It breaks early and recovers by update 36.
- **A tiny Tülu-style set** (A10): weaker identity; it still claims another lab in 9 of 52 thinking-ON answers.
- **Linear merges of A3 and A8a:** no blend gets both A3's BFCL and A8a's clean reasoning.

## Models

A3, A8a and A13 are archived in private HF repos under open-athena, with recipe, data hashes and scores in each card:

- `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-PathB-A3-2026.10.30`
- `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-PathB-A8a-2026.10.30`
- `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Identity-PathB-A13-2026.10.30`

topics.title: [infra] cw-rno2a artifact setup stalls for 10+ minutes
topics.body:
The 2026-10-30 SkyRL nightly CatCount lane stalled during setup of its data artifact under `s3://marin-rno2a`. Attempt 1 logged the artifact at 15:31:39 UTC, made no further progress, and hit its 1,200-second deadline before training. Attempt 2 logged its artifact at 15:51:32 and did not reach the artifact status check until 16:01:34. It then trained through step 5 but hit the same deadline before completion. [OPD and Grug Megatron passed in this run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/41081324351); Grug's success shows the prior account-wide write suspension in #10777 was not persistent throughout this run.

Reproduce:
1. Open the [failed CatCount job](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/41081324351/job/124150921600) and compare the `Step = documents/cat-count-canary/...` and `Status documents/cat-count-canary/...` timestamps for attempts `a1` and `a2`.
2. Compare the [2026-10-28 passing run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/40718681048), where those messages had the same timestamp and CatCount completed in 702 seconds.

Expected: Artifact setup completes promptly so the training gate can finish within its 1,200-second budget. Inspect CoreWeave object-storage request latency and errors for the artifact paths and restore a green nightly run. The native log does not identify the blocked S3 request or show a provider error, so today's exact storage failure mode is unconfirmed. The 2026-10-29 write suspension in #10777 is related history, not an established cause for this run. Tracked failure: #10776.

Incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/902
